## Research Question

(Describe your research question here. Include why this question might be of interest.)

Hotel booking demand can be influenced by various factors, including seasonal patterns, room prices, customer composition and customer requirements.

Understanding these factors is important for hotels because it may help them better understand customer behaviour and manage their resources.

This project aims to investigate the factors associated with hotel booking demand using the Hotel Booking Demand dataset. In particular, we focus on four aspects:

1.The relationship between arrival months and reservation frequency
2.The distribution of average daily rates (ADR) 3.Differences in guest composition between City Hotels and Resort Hotels
4.Customer demand for car parking spaces

We aim to identify patterns and differences in booking demand and gain a better understanding of hotel customer behaviour.



## Data

(Briefly describe your dataset here - include a description of the key variables you will be investigating. 
Include a citation for your data. 
See http://libraryguides.vu.edu.au/c.php?g=386501&p=4347840 for guidance on proper citation for datasets. 
If you got your data off the web, make sure to state the retrieval date.)

This project uses the Hotel Booking Demand dataset, which contains hotel reservation records for two types of hotels: City Hotels and Resort Hotels.

The dataset includes information about hotel bookings, arrival dates, room prices and guest characteristics. Several key variables are selected for our investigation.

These include `arrival_date_month` and `arrival_date_year`, which describe the timing of hotel arrivals; `adr`, which represents the Average Daily Rate; `adults`, `children` and `babies`, which describe guest composition; and `required_car_parking_spaces`, which records the number of car parking spaces requested.

These variables allow us to explore seasonal booking patterns, room price distributions, differences in guest composition and customer parking requirements.

Before conducting the analysis, relevant variables were checked for missing values. The data were also processed to ensure that the variables were in suitable formats for analysis.

The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mojtaba142/hotel-booking

-3.1 Seasonal Booking Patterns
```{r, echo=FALSE}
hotel_data <- read_csv("data/hotel_booking.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

hotel_data %>%
  summarise(
    missing_month = sum(is.na(arrival_date_month)),
    missing_year = sum(is.na(arrival_date_year))
  )
sum(duplicated(hotel_data))

month_order <- c(
  "January", "February", "March", "April",
  "May", "June", "July", "August",
  "September", "October", "November", "December"
)

hotel_data <- hotel_data %>%
  mutate(
    arrival_date_month = factor(
      arrival_date_month,
      levels = month_order,
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(arrival_date_month),
    !is.na(arrival_date_year)
  )

hotel_data %>%
  filter(is_canceled == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = arrival_date_month)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "tomato") +
  labs(
    title = "Cancelled Reservations by Arrival Month",
    x = "Arrival month",
    y = "Number of cancelled reservations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

hotel_data %>%
  filter(is_canceled == 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = arrival_date_month)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Non-cancelled Reservations by Arrival Month",
    x = "Arrival month",
    y = "Number of reservations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

monthly_reservations <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(is_canceled == 0) %>%
  count(arrival_date_month, name = "reservations") %>%
  arrange(desc(reservations))

monthly_reservations
```

In this part, we look at how the number of hotel reservations changes in different months. We use a bar chart to show the number of reservations in each month.

As shown in the Figure 1, August has the highest number of reservations, with around 13,800 bookings. January has the lowest number, with around 5,900 bookings. The number of reservations generally increases from January to May. It drops slightly in June, but increases again in July and August. After August, the number of bookings starts to decrease. November and December have much fewer reservations than the summer months.

From the chart, we can see that more people book hotels during the summer, especially in August. In comparison, there are fewer bookings during the winter months. This may be because more people choose to travel during the summer holidays.

-3.2 Room Price Distribution
```{r, echo=FALSE}
hotel_clean <- hotel_data %>%
	filter(adr > 0)
ggplot(hotel_clean, aes(x = adr)) +
geom_histogram(fill = "skyblue",
               color = "white",
               binwidth = 30,
	             boundary = 0)+
stat_bin(binwidth = 30, 
           boundary = 0, 
           geom = "text", 
           aes(label = after_stat(count)), 
           vjust = -0.5, 
           size = 3) +
xlim(0,400) +
facet_wrap(~hotel) +
labs(
	title = "Figure2:Distribution of ADR in City Hotels and Resort Hotels", 
	x = "ADR", 
	y = "reservation frequency"
)
```

In this part, we look at the relationship between ADR and the number of reservations for City Hotels and Resort Hotels. We use histograms to compare the distribution of ADR in the two types of hotels.

As shown in Figure 2, most City Hotel reservations have an ADR between around £60 and £150. The highest frequency is found between £60 and £90. For Resort Hotels, most reservations have a lower ADR, mainly between around £30 and £100. The number of reservations generally decreases as ADR increases in both types of hotels.

Overall, the chart shows that City Hotels tend to have higher ADR values than Resort Hotels. This suggests that the two types of hotels have different room price ranges and booking patterns.

-3.3 Guest Composition
```{r, echo=FALSE}
hotel_data <- read_csv("data/hotel_booking.csv",
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

guest_data <- hotel_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(adults),
         !is.na(children),
         !is.na(babies),
         adults + children + babies > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    guest_group = case_when(
      children > 0 & babies > 0 ~ "With both",
      children > 0 ~ "With children only",
      babies > 0 ~ "With babies only",
      TRUE ~ "Adults only"
    )
  )

guest_summary <- guest_data %>%
  count(hotel, guest_group) %>%
  group_by(hotel) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

print(guest_summary)

ggplot(guest_summary,
       aes(x = "", y = percentage, fill = guest_group)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  facet_wrap(~ hotel) +

geom_text(
  aes(label = ifelse(
    percentage >= 0.05,
    scales::percent(percentage, accuracy = 0.1),
    ""
  )),
  position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
  size = 3
) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure3:Guest Composition by Hotel Type",
    fill = "Guest Group"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

In this part, we compare the different guest groups in City Hotels and Resort Hotels. We divide the guests into four groups based on the numbers of adults, children and babies. Pie charts are used to show the percentage of each group.

As shown in Figure 3, adults only is the largest group in both types of hotels. It makes up 93.2% of City Hotel bookings and 90.2% of Resort Hotel bookings. The percentage of guests with children only is higher in Resort Hotels (8.4%) than in City Hotels (6.4%).

Overall, the results show that most hotel bookings are made by adults travelling without children or babies. Resort Hotels have a slightly higher percentage of guests travelling with children. This may suggest that Resort Hotels are more popular with families.

-3.4 Customer Parking Requirements
```{r, echo=FALSE}
hotel_bookings <- read_csv("data/hotel_booking.csv") 
parking_by_hotel <- hotel_bookings %>%
group_by(hotel) %>%
summarise(
total_parking = sum(required_car_parking_spaces, na.rm = TRUE)
)
ggplot(parking_by_hotel, aes(x = hotel, 
               y = total_parking)) +
geom_col() +
labs(
        title = "Figure4:Total Car Parking Spaces Required by Hotel Type",
        x = "Hotel Type",
        y = "Total Parking Spaces"
)
parking_by_month <- hotel_bookings %>%
mutate(
              arrival_date_month = factor(
              arrival_date_month,
              levels = month.name
            )
) %>%
group_by(arrival_date_year, arrival_date_month) %>%
summarise(
                    total_parking = sum(required_car_parking_spaces, na.rm = TRUE)
)
ggplot(parking_by_month, aes(x = arrival_date_month,
                     y = total_parking,
                     group = arrival_date_year,
                     colour = factor(arrival_date_year))) +
geom_line() +
geom_point() +
labs(
        title = "Figure5:Monthly Car Parking Demand from 2015 to 2017",
        x = "Month",
        y = "Total Parking Spaces",
        colour = "Year"
)
```

In this part, we investigate the demand for car parking spaces at City Hotels and Resort Hotels. We use a bar chart to compare the total parking spaces required by the two hotel types. We also use a line chart to show how parking demand changes across different months and years.

As shown in Figure 4, Resort Hotels require around 4,750 parking spaces, while City Hotels require around 1,950. This shows that the total parking demand for Resort Hotels is much higher than for City Hotels.

Figure 5 shows the monthly changes in parking demand from 2015 to 2017. In 2016, parking demand reaches its highest point in August, with around 450 spaces requested. In 2015, the highest demand is in October, while in 2017, it is in April. We can also see that parking demand changes across different months and years.

Overall, the results show that Resort Hotels have a higher total demand for parking spaces. There are also differences in monthly parking demand between different years. These results may help hotels understand their customers' parking needs and prepare enough parking spaces.

-3.5 Discussion and Conclusion
Overall, our analysis shows that City Hotels and Resort Hotels have some differences in booking patterns and customer characteristics. August has the highest number of reservations, while January has the lowest. City Hotels generally have higher ADR values, while Resort Hotels have more guests travelling with children and a higher demand for parking spaces.

However, our investigation also has some limitations. We only focused on four factors, and other factors such as booking cancellations and length of stay were not included. Also, our analysis shows patterns in the data but cannot prove that these factors directly affect hotel booking demand. The parking data for different years also cover different months, which makes comparisons more difficult.

Despite these limitations, this project has helped us understand the differences between City Hotels and Resort Hotels. It also shows that seasonal patterns, room prices, guest groups and parking requirements are useful factors to consider when studying hotel booking demand.
